question: Is the Amazon close to a tipping point beyond which much of it turns to savanna?
answer: The forest makes much of its own rain, so clearing weakens the rain the rest depends on. Lovejoy and Nobre put the threshold at 20 to 25% deforestation, and about 17% was already gone. Boulton and colleagues found satellite signs of falling resilience across more than three-quarters of the forest since the early 2000s.
move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether the rain feedback works locally or basin-wide.
counterpoint: The threshold is an argument from models, and the models disagree: many show dieback only under severe warming, and extra CO2 helps trees save water. Flores and colleagues project 10 to 47% of the forest exposed to compounding stresses by 2050, grave but patchy, region by region. A single basin-wide flip is not what the evidence shows.
reference: Lovejoy & Nobre, Amazon tipping point, Science Advances, 2018; Boulton, Lenton & Boers, Pronounced loss of Amazon rainforest resilience since the early 2000s, Nature Climate Change, 2022; Flores et al., Critical transitions in the Amazon forest system, Nature, 2024
